questions.question: What are the data binding types in Angular, and when do you use each?
questions.title: Angular Data Binding Types
questions.direct_answer: Angular has four binding types: interpolation ({{ }}) displays a component value in the template one-way; property binding ([prop]="expr") sets a DOM/component property one-way; event binding ((event)="handler") listens for DOM/component events and runs a handler; two-way binding ([(ngModel)]="prop") binds both directions, syncing input and a component property. Interpolation and property binding are one-way (component → view); event binding is one-way (view → component); two-way combines both. Use interpolation for display, property for setting attributes/inputs, event for reacting to user actions, and two-way for form inputs that update state.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can name all four binding types and their directions, and pick the right one for a given need (display vs set vs react vs sync).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using only interpolation and missing property/event binding, or confusing the bracket directions ([prop] is in, (event) is out).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Four types: interpolation ({{ }} display), property ([prop] set), event ((event) react), two-way ([(ngModel)] sync). Know the direction of each.

sections.title: Four Bindings, Four Directions
sections.content: Angular connects the component class to the template with four binding types. Interpolation ({{ value }}) flows one-way from component to view to display a value. Property binding ([property]="expr") flows one-way from component to view to set a DOM or component property. Event binding ((event)="handler()") flows one-way from view to component when a DOM or component event fires. Two-way binding ([(ngModel)]="prop") combines both, keeping an input and a component property in sync. The bracket notation encodes the direction: [ ] means target a property (data in), ( ) means listen to an event (data out), and [()] means both.

sections.title: The Four Binding Directions
sections.content:
Interpolation and property binding push data from component to view; event binding pulls from view to component; two-way does both.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  C[Component] -->|"{{ }}" / [prop]| V[View]
  V -->|"(event)"| C
  C <-->|"[(ngModel)]"| V
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Forgetting that [ ] is property (data in) and ( ) is event (data out) — the brackets encode direction.
Using interpolation where property binding is needed (can't bind to non-string properties via {{ }}).
Two-way binding without importing FormsModule (ngModel requires it).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Four binding types: interpolation ({{ }}), property ([prop]), event ((event)), two-way ([(ngModel)]).
Direction is in the brackets: [ ] = data in (property), ( ) = data out (event), [()] = both.
Use interpolation for display, property for setting inputs/attributes, event for reacting, two-way for form sync.
Interpolation and property binding are both one-way component→view; event is one-way view→component.
Two-way binding (ngModel) requires FormsModule — a common gotcha.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: Angular has four data binding types that connect the component to the template. Interpolation, the double curly braces, flows one-way from component to view to display a value. Property binding, the square brackets, sets a DOM or component property one-way from component to view. Event binding, the parentheses, flows one-way from view to component when an event fires. And two-way binding, the banana-in-a-box syntax, combines both to keep an input and a component property in sync. The bracket notation encodes the direction: square brackets mean target a property, data in; parentheses mean listen to an event, data out; and both together mean two-way. Use interpolation for display, property binding for setting attributes and inputs, event binding for reacting to user actions, and two-way for form inputs that update state. The common mistakes are confusing the bracket directions and using two-way binding without importing the FormsModule, which ngModel requires.
